transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2025-11-05 14:30 UTC
- Duration: ~58 minutes
- Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Dana Ortiz (Cygnus SRE Lead), Samir Khan (Cygnus CTO), Lina Park (Cygnus Product Ops)

Summary:
Redwood team walked through the Oct 28th outage postmortem for Cygnus Health. Root cause identified as a combination of KV-cache eviction pattern under unexpected prefix distribution plus a degraded autoscaler decision leading to transient OOMs on a subset of serving pods. Discussed short-term mitigations (prefix pinning, aggressive caching TTLs, heuristic-based autoscaler guardrails) and longer-term reliability improvements (dedicated pool, formal chaos tests, enhanced tracing). Customer asked for concrete timelines, contract ramifications, and security artifacts.

Topics covered:
- Incident timeline and root cause
- Immediate mitigations already applied
- Dedicated vs hosted fallback tradeoffs and cost implications
- Compliance and audit evidence requested by Cygnus
- Next steps, benchmarks, and follow-up meeting cadence

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Chen: Hi everyone, thanks for joining — I know we have a lot to get through. We wanted to run through the postmortem from Oct 28, what we changed, and the plan to prevent recurrence.
[00:18] Dana Ortiz: Thanks Alex. Yeah, that outage hit our production workflows pretty hard. We saw a spike in 5xx and our downstream job queue backed up. We appreciate the quick patch but we need the full postmortem and to understand how this won't happen again.
[00:30] Maya Singh: Totally, thanks Dana. We'll start with the timeline. So at ~09:12 UTC we started seeing elevated error rates; by 09:16 a subset of pods began evicting KV cache entries because the prefix distribution suddenly shifted. That, combined with the autoscaler's pod churn — it tried to scale down and then back up, created pressure on memory allocations which led to OOMs on two pods, and the fallback routing didn't fully kick in because the model variant mapping was slightly misaligned.
[01:05] Samir Khan: Can you clarify "prefix distribution"? Is that the request surface we saw from our clients, or something internal?
[01:12] Maya Singh: It's how the runtime stores key/value cache per prompt prefix. Normally the hotspots are stable, but your prefix fan-out increased due to a new templated prompt a team rolled out; many different prefixes meant smaller KV hits and more memory pressure. The cache eviction policy then started thrashing.
[01:30] Dana Ortiz: Right, that change was rolled out at 08:50 by our Search team. We didn't anticipate the fan-out. We have the change log if that helps.
[01:40] Alex Chen: That helps a lot, Dana. We correlated your change log with trace ids you shared and saw the same pattern. We have a doc with the traces — link: https://redwood.internal/incident/4521/traces (note: internal link in transcript).
[01:56] Lina Park: Quick Q — what about the autoscaler? Was that behavior expected?
[02:03] Maya Singh: The autoscaler is tuned with heuristics for throughput and memory headroom. In this case rapid change in working set made the heuristic oscillate. We have guardrails but the specific combo of prefix fan-out + scale-down window caused the two nodes to drop needed shards.
[02:20] Dana Ortiz: Ok. So what's the short-term fix we can deploy while you work on a long-term plan?
[02:26] Maya Singh: Short term we applied three things: 1) increased cache TTLs for the hot prefix ranges to avoid thrash, 2) set an autoscaler minimum replica floor for your pool for the next 72 hours, and 3) adjusted the fallback mapping so requests route to a compatible variant when the pool is under pressure. These were live by ~11:00 UTC.
[02:52] Samir Khan: Did that restore stability?
[02:55] Maya Singh: Yes, error rates dropped back to baseline and OOMs stopped. But it's remedial; we want a more robust solution so this doesn't repeat.
[03:05] Alex Chen: For medium-term, we recommend testing on a dedicated pool and a model profile with a pinned cache config. That reduces noisy neighbor risk and gives predictable SLOs. We'll share pricing delta for a 3-month pilot.
[03:20] Dana Ortiz: The thing Cygnus cares about is predictability and compliance. How quickly can you stand up dedicated capacity?
[03:28] Maya Singh: We can provision a dedicated GPU pool in your hosted region within 3-5 business days for a pilot, depending on commit. The operational change is minimal, and we can pin the model version and cache config.
[03:40] Lina Park: What's the cost delta?
[03:42] Alex Chen: I'll send the pricing matrix after this call; rough order magnitude is in the follow-up email but we can put a proposal for a short-term reserved cap that covers your high-critical traffic windows.
[03:55] Dana Ortiz: We also need SOC2 artifacts and the network diagram to present to our security and procurement.
[04:01] Alex Chen: Understood — we'll share SOC2, ISO certs, and the architecture/network diagram by EOD tomorrow. Link to docs: https://redwood.com/security (public) and we'll attach the network diagram in the follow-up.
[04:16] Samir Khan: Two things — one, during the incident the fallback mapping didn't fully route to the fallback variant. Was that a config mismatch or a bug?
[04:25] Maya Singh: It was a config mismatch at the model-variant alias layer; the canary mapping we'd pushed earlier didn't include the precise alias your routing expects. We've fixed the alias and added validation to prevent variant alias mismatches during rollouts.
[04:40] Dana Ortiz: Good. Second — we saw a spike in latency on the fallback path. Is that expected?
[04:45] Maya Singh: Some increased tail latency is expected when falling back to a different variant, but the spike you saw was larger due to cold KV cache on the fallback. We're adding proactive prefix-warmup for fallbacks to reduce that impact.
[04:58] Alex Chen: For long-term reliability improvements we're proposing: 1) dedicated pool option, 2) improved autoscaler guardrails and hysteresis tuning, 3) chaos testing with your production-like workload every release, 4) better tracing and alerting around KV-cache miss rates, and 5) a runbook with explicit operator steps.
[05:20] Samir Khan: The chaos testing — can Redwood run that or do we need to create it?
[05:24] Maya Singh: We can run a joint chaos exercise. We'll supply the harness and run with your SRE; that would be recommended before any major rollout.
[05:33] Dana Ortiz: OK let's talk timing. We need the bench results and the mitigations in place before our Q4 compliance review on Dec 2.
[05:41] Alex Chen: Noted. We'll prioritize the bench and the KV-cache playbook — aiming to deliver the playbook and bench plan next week.
[05:50] Lina Park: Are there any immediate changes on our side? We'll need to communicate to product teams about templated prompts.
[05:58] Maya Singh: Yes, please hold the rollout of the templated prompt until we validate the dedicated-pool bench. If immediate rollouts are necessary, we recommend throttling the template variants and adding a prefix-affinity header so we can pin cache shards.
[06:15] Dana Ortiz: We'll do that.
[06:18] Alex Chen: Quick note: we also logged this incident into your support case: support.redwood.com/cases/4521. We'll attach the detailed postmortem doc and the trace artifacts.
[06:30] Samir Khan: On the procurement side, if we move to a dedicated pool, what's the minimum commit?
[06:36] Alex Chen: For pilot it's a short-term reserved commitment; we'll outline tiers in the pricing email. For long-term commitments we can discuss month-to-month vs annual discounts.
[06:45] Dana Ortiz: Anything else?
[06:47] Maya Singh: One small technical note — we're rolling out a change to the autoscaler code that will add a 30s stabilization window for memory-based scaling decisions and increase the eviction grace to reduce shard thrash. We plan to push this to canary next week and to all pools after successful validation.
[07:10] Dana Ortiz: Sounds good. Please coordinate the canary schedule with our on-call.
[07:15] Alex Chen: Will do.
[07:18] Lina Park: Recap for us please — what are the next steps and owners?
[07:20] Alex Chen: Sure: Maya will run the dedicated-pool bench and share results (Owner: Maya, Due: 2025-11-12). Alex will send pricing and contract amendment draft (Owner: Alex, Due: 2025-11-10). Cygnus (Dana) will share offending traces and logs (Owner: Dana, Due: 2025-11-06). We'll provide SOC2 and network diagram (Owner: Alex, Due: 2025-11-06).
[07:45] Samir Khan: Ok that timeline works.
[07:48] Dana Ortiz: Appreciate the thoroughness, team. We'll hold the templated prompt rollout till after the bench.
[07:55] Alex Chen: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the email that includes links and attachments. If anything urgent comes up, ping the AE/SE pair.
[08:05] (call ends)

Attachments & links referenced:
- Postmortem doc: https://redwood.internal/incident/4521/postmortem (internal)
- Support case: https://support.redwood.com/cases/4521
- Security docs (public): https://redwood.com/security
- Note: customer will provide change log and traces via shared S3 link after the call.

Recap (short):
- Root cause: KV-cache eviction thrash + autoscaler oscillation triggered by new templated prompt fan-out; led to OOMs on subset of pods and elevated 5xx.
- Short-term mitigations: increased cache TTLs, autoscaler floor, fallback alias fix, prefix-warmup for fallback.
- Medium/long-term: dedicated pool pilot, autoscaler hysteresis change, chaos testing, improved tracing, runbook.
- Immediate deliverables: KV-cache mitigation playbook, dedicated-pool benchmark, SOC2/network diagram, pricing/contract draft.
